You learn the ～ない form and use it to ask someone NOT to do something (～ないで ください), to say what you must do (～なければ なりません) and what you don’t need to do (～なくても いい です).

To form the ～ない form (the plain negative) for every group.
To ask for something NOT to be done: ～ないで ください.
To say what you must do: ～なければ なりません.
To say what you DON’T need to do: ～なくても いい です.
To use まで に (deadline) differently from まで (until, duration).
Packing for Japan
It’s the evening before the departure. Yuki comes round to Ana’s to check the suitcase, because Ana and Mihai are leaving for Japan tomorrow morning.
Ana, your passport? Please don’t forget it.
It’s here. It’s fine.
Yuki, do we have to get a visa?
No, Spaniards and Romanians don’t need to get a visa.
Good! Do we have to take lots of cash?
Take a little. Because the inn only takes cash. But everywhere else you can use a card.
What do I do with my medicines?
Don’t put them in the suitcase. Put them in your bag and take them on the plane with you.
Oh, and an umbrella? Does it rain a lot in Japan?
It doesn’t rain much in November. You don’t need to take an umbrella. You can also buy one at a convenience store.
What time do we have to be at the airport by?
The plane is at ten, so get there by seven. Don’t be late!
Mihai, have you packed your charger?
Ah…! I forgot. I’ll go and get it right away!
Hee-hee. Plugs in Japan are different from the ones in Spain, so don’t forget the adapter either!

“-nai” sounds like English “nigh”: たべない = ta-be-nai. It’s the plain negative form, used between friends.
Long, but rhythmic: na-ke-re-ba na-ri-ma-sen. In fast speech Japanese people say “-nakya” (いかなきゃ), but you say it in full.
Verbs in -います gain a w: かいます → かわない, はらいます → はらわない. Not “かあない”!
1. The ～ない form: the plain negative
Just as ～ません is the polite negative, ～ない is the plain negative (between friends, and in many grammar structures). It’s formed like this:
the -i sound before ます becomes -a + ない
Group 1 (in -い)
-い becomes -わ + ない ⚠️
drop ます, add ない
The most important exception: あります → ない (not “あらない”!). “I don’t have any money” = おかね が ない.
Group 1: the “i” row moves to the “a” row: き→か, み→ま, し→さ, ち→た, り→ら, び→ば, ぎ→が. And い→わ.
2. Please don’t…: ～ないで ください
The ～ない form + で ください = a request NOT to do something. It’s the negative partner of ～て ください (chapter 9):
Do it!
Don’t do it!
いれて ください (put it in)
いれないで ください (don’t put it in)
きて ください (come)
こないで ください (don’t come)
しんぱい しないで ください (don’t worry)
Please don’t smoke here.
Between friends, without ください: わすれないで! (Don’t forget!).
3. Must: ～なければ なりません
Literally: “if you don’t do it, it won’t do”. Take the ～ない form, drop い and add ければ なりません:
I have to go.
I have to take my medicine.
Tomorrow I have to get up early.
You’ll also hear ～なければ いけません. It means exactly the same.
Don’t translate “must” with できます or いい. “Must” = ～なければ なりません, a fixed expression.
4. You don’t need to…: ～なくても いい です
Take the ～ない form, drop い and add くても いい です (“even if you don’t, it’s fine”):
You don’t need to get a visa.
You don’t need to come tomorrow.
Yes, you must
No, you don’t need to
5. まで vs まで に
until (the action LASTS until then)
じゅうじ まで ねます (I sleep until ten)
by (a deadline; the action happens ONCE before then)
じゅうじ まで に きて ください (come by ten)
I have to return the book by Friday.
The typical mistake: “しちじ まで くうこう に ついて ください”. Correct with まで に, because arriving is a moment, not a duration.

ながい いちにち — A very long day
Five in the morning. The alarm clock rang. Today is the day they leave for Japan.
Mihai got up straight away. Today he mustn’t oversleep.
He took a shower, washed his face and opened his suitcase once more.
Passport, there. Medicines, there. Charger… there. Adapter… not there!
“Oh no! I have to buy an adapter!”
But it’s half past five in the morning. The shops aren’t open yet.
Mihai sent Ana a message. “I haven’t got an adapter! What do I do?”
The answer came straight away. “Don’t worry! You can buy one at the airport.”
Six o’clock. There was a knock at the door. It was Mrs Suzuki.
“Mihai, please take this with you.”
It was a small bag. Inside there was a lucky charm and a letter.
“The letter is for my younger sister in Kyoto. Please meet her for me.”
“But please don’t open it until you get to Kyoto.”
Before seven, Mihai and Ana arrived at the airport.
Yuki and Kenji had come to see them off too.
Kenji gave them a big bag. “Eat these on the plane. They’re onigiri.”
“Kenji, the food on the plane is free…” “Because plane food isn’t tasty!”
At the check-in counter, a problem came up.
“Sir, the suitcase weighs 28 kilos. The limit is 23.”
It was Ana’s suitcase.
“What have you got in there?” asked Mihai.
“Clothes… shoes… souvenirs for everyone… five books…”
“Five books?!”
Ana took out three books. Yuki took them.
“I’ll keep them for you. Don’t worry.”
This time it was 22 kilos. “That’s fine. Here you are.”
At a shop in the airport, Mihai bought an adapter.
There was just one adapter for Japan. The last one.
“Great! I’m lucky today!”
In front of the boarding gate, they all said goodbye.
“Have a good trip! Send lots of photos!” said Yuki.
“Say hello to my wife. Don’t eat too much okonomiyaki!” said Kenji.
“See you!”
On the plane, Mihai looked at Mrs Suzuki’s bag.
He wants to open it. But he mustn’t. Because he promised.
Next to him, Ana was already asleep, with one of Kenji’s onigiri in her hand.
The fourteen-hour journey had begun.
Outside the window there were lots of white clouds. Madrid was already very far away.
Mihai closed his eyes and thought about what he wanted to do in Japan. See Fuji. Get into a hot spring. Read more kanji.
And, without realising it, Mihai fell asleep too.
